sources.citation: Kellogg, S. H. 1893. A grammar of the Hindi language.. also the colloquial dialects of Rajputana, Kumaon, Avadh.. 2nd ed. London: Kegan Paul. (Mewari treated among the Rajputana dialects.)
sources.note: Only a general Hindi remark (sec. 35: accent exists but is weak and subordinate to quantity; sec. 415 accent in causal verbs); nothing specific to Mewari.
'There are 31 consonants, 10 vowels and 2 diphthongs in Mewari. Intonation is prominent.' Nothing on stress placement (text mirrors the Gusain 2013 blurb).

sources.citation: Ghatage, A. M. 1962. Historical linguistics and Indo-Aryan languages. Bombay: University of Bombay. (pp. 65-69 on Allen's Marwari/Mewari/Harauti labial data.)
sources.note: Nothing on Mewari stress; methodological discussion of bh/b/v correspondences.

sources.citation: Allen, W. S. 1957. Some phonological characteristics of Rajasthani. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 20: 5-11. (First-hand 1952 fieldwork on Harauti, Mewari [Udaipur and 'Southern Mewari'] and Marwari.)
sources.note: No word-stress statement. Mewari data concern aspiration (p. 6: Udaipur has no non-initial voiced aspirates; S. Mewari no non-initial aspiration), and p. 6 sec. 1(iv)(b): in S. Mewari loss of non-initial *s>h yields 'a lengthening of the preceding vowel together with a rising pitch-pattern' ([haaro] 'mother-in-law's house' vs [haro] 'brother-in-law'), also in Mewari future forms. Silent on accent placement.

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed.) 1908. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. IX: Indo-Aryan family, Central group, Part II: Specimens of the Rajasthani and Gujarati. Calcutta. 'Mewari' pp. 78-89.
sources.note: Nothing. Mewari section (pp. 78-79) gives grammatical notes (genitive -ko, postpositions, verb forms) and a Parable specimen; no pronunciation/accent paragraph. In the whole volume 'accent' occurs only in the transliteration key.

sources.citation: D'Souza, Royson Norman. 2025. A Descriptive Phonology of Mewari. In: Proceedings of the 15th Payap University National Research Conference 2025 (in cooperation with UNRN and APHEIT), 14 February 2025, linguistics group, pp. 312-324. Chiang Mai: Payap University Research Office.
sources.note: Phonology sketch: 31 consonants, 8 oral vowels + nasal counterparts, syllable template (C)(C)V(C)(C), geminates, retroflex harmony, and a 'Stress' subsection (p. 323) stating stress is not contrastive, final syllable stressed in isolation forms. No tone inventory or tonal analysis is proposed for Mewari; tone appears only on p. 316, where the reduction/loss of breathy-voiced stops in Mewari is compared with Panjabi (which 'replaced them with tonal contrasts') versus Gujarati and Sindhi, and Mewari is said to pattern like Sindhi (mild implosion of modal voiced stops), i.e. no tonal reflex is r…

tone.quote: Stress does not appear to be contrastive in Mewari. When words are spoken in isolation the final syllable tends to be stressed. In connected speech, some words appear to lose their stress. Further research is required to confirm these observations and to identify the precise phonetic correlates of stress in Mewari. /ɡat̪i/ [ɡaˈt̪i] 'shawl' /bad̪ i/ [baˈd̪ i] 'fat'
tone.locator: p. 323, section 5, subsection 'Stress'; tone comparison with Panjabi/Sindhi on p. 316
tone.summary: No lexical tone described; stress non-contrastive (final syllable stressed in citation forms, weakened in connected speech); breathy-voiced stops reduced/lost mostly without a reported tonal reflex (patterning with Sindhi implosion, not Panjabi tonogenesis).
